title: Examining the impact of lesion location and extent on post-stroke neuroplasticity
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it seeks to understand the mechanisms associated
with recovery from stroke, which is the leading cause of disability in the US. Because our ability to understand
the mechanisms of post-stroke recovery has been limited by differences between patients in the location and
extent of their strokes, this study will specifically examine the impact of lesion location and extent on the
mechanisms of post-stroke recovery. The results will provide critical information needed to develop novel,
patient-specific therapies to restore function after brain injury.

title: Administrative Supplement: Enhancing cell-type-specific inference with millions of snRNA-seq and deep learning methods
text:
The proposed study will employ innovative deep learning (DL) models to enhance the inference
of cell-type-specific gene expression profiles of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD), aiming to identify
profiles that are associated to disease progression and regional vulnerability. Additionally, we
will investigate cell-type-specific gene co-expression networks to uncover interaction patterns
related to AD pathogenesis. This comprehensive approach will provide a detailed molecular-
level analysis, furthering our understanding of the complex mechanisms underlying AD.

title: DESIGN  AND  FABRICATION  OF  A  SOFT  PARALLEL  ROBOT  FOR TRANSCATHETER INTERVENTIONS
text:
Robotic catheter technology has the potential to revolutionize the treatment of cardiac disease. However, the
existing catheter systems cannot provide the high level of maneuverability that is required for cardiovascular
intervention. To address this issue, the current work proposes a novel six degrees of freedom transcatheter
robotics system. Upon successful completion of this project, the heart surgeons will have access to a novel
efficient device to plan and study new procedures for transcatheter heart surgery. Heart failure is a chronic
disease, causing disruption to the lives of sufferers and their families. Developing this new device can reduce
the impact of heart failure on the lives of the patient and those around them, and it helps to lengthen life and
promote a healthy society.

title: Impacts of Neighborhood Contexts and Medicaid Policy on Lung Cancer Survival in Low-SES Patients
text: Although poor lung cancer survival in low-income people is well documented, the influential factors of lung cancer care in this population remain unclear. In the population-based cohorts of lung cancer patients insured with Medicaid, we will assess the impacts of neighborhood contexts, Medicaid policies, and hospitals on cancer-directed treatment, tobacco cessation treatment, and cancer outcomes. The results will enhance our understanding of how neighborhood contexts, Medicaid policy, and hospitals affect lung cancer care and survival in low-income populations, and will also help identify modifiable targets for future multilevel lung cancer interventions.

title: The Role of Tomosyn-1 in Regulating Insulin Secretion from Pancreatic beta-cells
text:
Diabetes is a serious public health problem in the United States that affects more than 29 million people.
Reduction in insulin secretion from pancreatic beta cells causes diabetes. The proposed project improves our
fundamental knowledge of how beta cells secrete insulin to maintain blood glucose levels and aligns with the
mission of NIH to find the treatment for Type 2 diabetes.

title: The Metabolic Crossroads: Decoding Fentanyl's Impact on HIV/HBV Co-infection for Targeted Interventions
text:
HIV/HBV co-infection accelerates liver disease progression and increases cancer risk in people living with both
viruses. Fentanyl use may create additional dangerous complications by potentially interfering with antiviral drug
metabolism and causing life-threatening drug interactions. Using innovative primary cell culture models and
humanized mice, we will determine how fentanyl exposure affects HIV/HBV co-infection biology and drug
interactions. These studies will provide critical information for managing HIV/HBV co-infection in people with
substance use disorders and may help develop safer treatment strategies.

title: Developing Human Pluripotent Stem Cell Tools for Region-Specific Pain Circuits
text:
Neither conventional preclinical models using rodents nor simple human stem cell models using pain-sensing
nociceptors capture the complexity of human pain circuits. This hampers the discovery of solutions for
treatment of chronic pain, which may potentially target multiple cell types (including both neurons and
supporting glia), localized cell populations with distinct positional identities and/or the environment where these
pain networks reside. This proposal will develop advanced human stem cell tools that will establish region-
specific cells, circuits, and tissues, enhancing our fundamental understanding of human pain networks along
the body axis and accelerating the creation of accurate models that can be used for high throughput drug
screening.

title: Development of A High Throughput Image-Guided IMRT System forPreclinical Research
text:
A major impediment in translating animal radiation studies to human patients is the disparity in radiation
techniques. Existing methods cannot create human like conformal radiation dose on mice with necessary
accuracy and efficiency. To better mimic human treatment without prohibitively complicated and slow procedures,
we propose to develop a high throughput image guided small animal conformal irradiation platform.

title: An Integrative Approach to the Etiology of Internalizing Disorders in the Lifelines Cohort
text:
This project seeks to clarify the etiology of key internalizing psychiatric disorders and closely associated
functional medical disorders by applying a range of methods from epidemiology, genetic epidemiology
and molecular genetics to the large informative population-based cohort in the Netherlands called
Lifelines. We will attempt to understand the origins of the comorbidity between these disorders and
how genes and environment contribute to their development. To meet these goals, we will apply
advanced statistical methods to a unique set of epidemiological and molecular genetic resources.

title: Research Education Core
text: The Research Education Core (REC) of the H-H U54 is committed to advancing cancer research education at Howard University (HU) and strengthening the national cancer research workforce. Building on the longstanding collaboration between HU and Johns Hopkins University (JHU), the Core will implement integrated research and educational programs that leverage the complementary strengths of both institutions. Key initiatives include the establishment of a joint Ph.D. program in Medical Physics, the implementation of the “School2Lab” initiative to engage rising junior and senior STEM students from regional high schools, and the development of innovative coursework focused on the applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning in cancer research and education. These initiatives will be delivered through the Research Opportunity and Innovation at Johns Hopkins and Howard Universities (ROI@J-HU) training framework, which supports structured mentorship, early research engagement, and cross-institution collaboration. Collectively, these efforts aim to expand access to advanced training in oncology and biomedical sciences, while preparing a skilled and well-equipped workforce to address emerging challenges in cancer research and care.

title: PET Imaging to Define Mechanisms and Stratify Risk in Arrhythmogenic Cardiomyopathy
text:
The proposed research is relevant to the NIH because it is focused on fundamental biology that will impact
cardiovascular disease by defining how inflammation drives arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy (ACM), a major
cause of sudden death in young patients. By using PET imaging to image and quantify inflammation in
preclinical models, this work will establish a non-invasive imaging approach to detect and predict ACM disease
progression. Ultimately, these findings will lay the foundation for future strategies to stratify risk and develop
targeted therapies that prevent sudden cardiac death.

title: Leveraging the metastatic tumor stroma to limit breast cancer progression
text:
Nontumor cells aid tumor cell growth and help tumor cells evade the immune system. We find that by inhibiting a
protein called p38MAPK in these non-tumor cells, we can reduce metastatic tumor growth. Because there are
many different types of nontumor cells in a growing metastatic tumor and we do not know which ones assist
incipient tumor cell growth and survival, the goal of this work is to identify the cells, learn how they help tumor
cells grow and use that information to design more potent anti-tumor therapies.

title: Deep learning technologies for estimating the optimal task performance of medical imaging systems
text:
There remains an important need for the development of effective, rapid and safe methods for developing and
refining new medical imaging technologies that can improve patient outcomes. Virtual imaging trials (VITs) hold
great potential for this purpose but, currently, their effectiveness is generally limited by the use of image quality
measures that do not quantify clinical utility for realistic diagnostic tasks. The proposed research will address
this and thereby enable highly effective VITs that will accelerate new medical imaging technologies towards
clinical use.

title: Dual-targeted DOTA CAR T cells with image-guided monitoring for solid tumor treatment
text:
Solid tumors are hard to treat with CAR T cells because the antigens they express are heterogenous. We
propose the clinical translation of an approach that synergizes clinical imaging with T cell therapy to overcome
the current limitations of toxicity, antigen loss variants and cost of engineered T cell therapy through the
application of a bio-orthogonal image-enabled adaptable CAR (ImAC) method where CAR T cells can be tracked
by imaging after infusion, and delivery of CAR T cells with tailored payloads can be monitored through
noninvasive imaging. We will optimize the ImAC method in rigorous preclinical assays and then test feasibility,
safety and response in a Phase I clinical trial for women with advanced ovarian cancer.

title: MetaDx: Rapid Diagnosis of Fungal, Bacterial, and Viral Infections Using Whole Metagenomic Sequencing
text:
Invasive fungal infections (IFIs) are a critical public health concern due to their difficult diagnosis and the
growing threat of antifungal resistance. This research aims to revolutionize the diagnosis of IFIs by utilizing
metagenomic sequencing and machine learning to rapidly identify pathogens and their resistance profiles,
allowing for earlier and more effective treatment. By improving diagnostic speed and accuracy, this approach
has the potential to significantly enhance patient outcomes, reduce the burden of IFIs on healthcare systems,
and decrease the need for broad-spectrum treatments that can contribute to the development of resistance.

title: AAV-Mediated Gene Silencing in Hibernating Muscle: A Pilot Study to Validate RBM3 Protection Against Disuse Atrophy
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because it focuses on molecular mechanisms involved
in muscle atrophy protection in a natural mammalian model of adaptation. Once such mechanisms are
determined, there is a potential for a significant improvement in interventions for disuse muscle atrophy.
Thus, the proposed study is relevant to the part of the NIH’s mission that is related to reducing illness and
disability.

title: Understanding how T cell intrinsic androgen receptor activity influences cell differentiation and dysfunction
text:
Testosterone is a powerful regulator of cell differentiation and disease. We have discovered a critical role for
androgen, of which the most common is testosterone, in limiting the effectiveness of immunotherapy in
prostate cancer. This extension aims to understand the mechanism(s) by which androgen receptor signaling in
CD8 T cells orchestrates T cell dysfunction.

title: Defined microbial communities to prevent and eradicate infection by AMR pathogens
text: Before the discovery of antibiotics, infectious diseases were the three leading causes of death in the United States and constituted nearly 50% of the deaths annually. Today only one infectious disease, pneumonia, is among the top 10 causes of death in the US, largely due to the success of antibiotics in treating bacterial infections. Unfortunately, the public health benefits provided by antibiotics are at serious risk due to the emergence of antibiotic resistant bacteria, an inevitable consequence of the evolutionary pressure exerted on bacteria by these drugs. Eventually the bacterial pathogens we hope to keep at bay will become resistant to all clinically relevant antibiotics, plunging humans back into a pre-antibiotic world in which infectious disease is the leading cause of death. Therefore, we need to find innovative, and rapidly implementable, ways to reduce or supplement antibiotics to preserve their utility in controlling bacterial infections. Many bacterial pathogens, termed pathobionts, reside within the human microbiota in the absence of disease and only instigate pathogenesis after disruption of the microbial community driven by abrupt environmental changes such as acute inflammation. While there is general acceptance that the commensal microbes provide pathogen colonization resistance and suppression of pathobiont virulence in a healthy state, the mechanistic understanding for how they provide these benefits is lacking. In this project, we explore using the human microbiome to identify ecological principles that allow for the design and implementation of microbial communities that suppress bacterial pathogens. We have selected Clostridioides difficile and extraintestinal pathogenic E. coli (ExPEC) as the two main pathogens to study as they are deemed antibiotic resistance threats by the CDC and necessitate millions of antibiotic prescriptions each year. Even with antibiotic treatment, recurrent infections with both of these pathogens is common, and there is currently a lack of long-lasting preventative strategies. Using a novel method to simplify human microbiome communities and advanced in vitro human tissue culture and humanized murine models, we seek to identify key microbial consortia for suppressing these pathogens. We ultimately expect to optimize a small number of defined microbial communities that can be used to eradicate or prevent these infections in people.

title: Multifunctional nanoparticles for improved immunotherapy of melanoma
text:
Project Narrative.
This project will evaluate a novel multifunctional ultrasound responsive nanomaterial platform in preclinical
studies to allow its clinical translation for improved immunotherapy of melanoma and potentially other cancers.
We hypothesize that our multifunctional nanomaterial platform can ablate solid tumors when insonated with low-
intensity focused ultrasound, releasing tumor antigens and inducing immunogenic cell death to generate innate
and adaptive immune responses. In addition, we will utilize these nanoparticles for sustained delivery of a TLR7/8
agonist to obtain a more robust and durable immune response.

title: AI2Equity: AI Integrating Social Determinants of Health to Advance Health Equity in Cardiovascular Risk Prediction
text:
AI2Equity: AI Integrating SDOH Data to Advance Health Equity in Cardiovascular Risk Prediction
Narrative
There is a pressing need to address health disparities in cardiovascular disease (CVD). This study will use
machine learning to develop a novel CVD risk prediction model that considers social determinants of health,
structural social factors, and clinical factors together, as well as their complex interactions. The model will be
designed to be equitable, interpretable, and generalizable across diverse populations.
